{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
In [[real analysis]] and [[measure theory]], the '''Vitali convergence theorem''', named after the [[Italy|Italian]] [[mathematician]] [[Giuseppe Vitali]], is a generalization of the better-known [[dominated convergence theorem]] of [[Henri Lebesgue]]. It is a characterization of the convergence in [[Lp space|''L<sup>p</sup>'']] in terms of convergence in measure and a condition related to [[uniform integrability]].

== Preliminary definitions ==
Let <math>(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> be a [[measure space]], i.e. <math>\mu : \mathcal{A}\to [0,\infty]</math> is a set function such that <math>\mu(\emptyset)=0</math> and <math>\mu</math> is countably-additive. All functions considered in the sequel will be functions <math>f:X\to \mathbb{K}</math>, where <math>\mathbb{K}=\R</math> or <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. We adopt the following definitions according to Bogachev's terminology.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Bogachev|first=Vladimir I.|title=Measure Theory Volume I|publisher=Springer|year=2007|isbn=978-3-540-34513-8|location=New York|pages=267-271}}</ref>

* A set of functions <math>\mathcal{F} \subset L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> is called '''uniformly integrable''' if <math>\lim_{M\to+\infty} \sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} \int_{\{|f|>M\}} |f|\, d\mu = 0</math>, i.e  <math>\forall\ \varepsilon >0,\ \exists\ M_\varepsilon>0
: \sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} \int_{\{|f|\geq M_\varepsilon\}} |f|\, d\mu < \varepsilon</math>.
* A set of functions <math>\mathcal{F} \subset L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> is said to have '''uniformly absolutely continuous integrals''' if <math>\lim_{\mu(A)\to 0}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} \int_A |f|\, d\mu = 0</math>, i.e. <math>\forall\ \varepsilon>0,\ \exists\ \delta_\varepsilon >0,\ \forall\ A\in\mathcal{A} : 
\mu(A)<\delta_\varepsilon \Rightarrow \sup_{f\in \mathcal{F}} \int_A |f|\, d\mu < \varepsilon</math>. This definition is sometimes used as a definition of uniform integrability. However, it differs from the definition of uniform integrability given above.


When <math>\mu(X)<\infty</math>, a set of functions <math>\mathcal{F} \subset L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> is uniformly integrable if and only if it is bounded in <math>L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> and has uniformly absolutely continuous integrals. If, in addition, <math>\mu</math> is atomless, then the uniform integrability is equivalent to the uniform absolute continuity of integrals.

== Finite measure case ==
Let <math>(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> be a measure space with <math>\mu(X)<\infty</math>. Let <math>(f_n)\subset L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> and <math>f</math> be an <math>\mathcal{A}</math>-measurable function. Then, the following are equivalent : 

# <math>f\in L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> and <math>(f_n)</math> converges to <math>f</math> in <math>L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> ;
# The sequence of functions <math>(f_n)</math> converges in <math>\mu</math>-measure to <math>f</math> and <math>(|f_n|^p)_{n\geq 1}</math> is uniformly integrable ;


For a proof, see Bogachev's monograph "Measure Theory, Volume I".<ref name=":0" />

==Infinite measure case==
Let <math>(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> be a measure space and <math>1\leq p<\infty</math>. Let <math>(f_n)_{n\geq 1} \subseteq L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> and <math>f\in L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math>. Then, <math>(f_n)</math> converges to <math>f</math> in <math>L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> if and only if the following holds :
# The sequence of functions <math>(f_n)</math> converges in <math>\mu</math>-measure to <math>f</math> ;
#<math>(f_n^p)</math> has uniformly absolutely continuous integrals;
# For every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, there exists <math>X_\varepsilon\in \mathcal{A}</math> such that <math>\mu(X_\varepsilon)<\infty</math> and  <math>\sup_{n\geq 1}\int_{X\setminus X_\varepsilon} |f_n|^p\, d\mu <\varepsilon.</math>
When <math>\mu(X)<\infty</math>, the third condition becomes superfluous (one can simply take <math>X_\varepsilon = X</math>) and the first two conditions give the usual form of Lebesgue-Vitali's convergence theorem originally stated for measure spaces with finite measure. In this case, one can show that conditions 1 and 2 imply that the sequence <math>(|f_n|^p)_{n\geq 1}</math> is uniformly integrable.

==Converse of the theorem==
Let <math>(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> be measure space. Let <math>(f_n)_{n\geq 1} \subseteq L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> and assume that <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_A f_n\,d\mu</math> exists for every <math>A\in\mathcal{A}</math>. Then, the sequence <math>(f_n)</math> is bounded in <math>L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> and has uniformly absolutely continuous integrals. In addition, there exists <math>f\in L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)</math> such that <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_A f_n\,d\mu = \int_A f\, d\mu</math> for every <math>A\in\mathcal{A}</math>.

When <math>\mu(X)<\infty</math>, this implies that <math>(f_n)</math> is uniformly integrable.

For a proof, see Bogachev's monograph "Measure Theory, Volume I".<ref name=":0" />
